itinerary.cal: Best done once the brushy approach and ridge are fully snow-free, typically mid-summer through early fall (roughly July-September).

days.note: This is a big single-day outing, not a backpack: parties bike or hike ~6-7 miles up the steep Skookum Pasture logging road, then scramble a brushy climbers' trail onto the ridge where the terrain turns to famously grippy olivine/dunite rock. The ridge itself is mostly 2nd-3rd class if you stay left/west of the crest, with short 3rd-4th class steps and real exposure near the top; route-finding (staying left, not straying right onto harder terrain) is the crux of the day as much as the climbing.
days.title: Car-to-car: Skookum Pasture road + olivine ridge scramble

schedule.label: Leave the car / gate
schedule.detail: Start hiking or pedaling the steep logging road while it's still dark to bank time.

schedule.label: Reach end of road / stash bike
schedule.detail: Road gives way to a brushy climbers' trail heading for the ridge base.

schedule.label: Gain the ridge crest
schedule.detail: Forest opens onto exposed olivine/dunite rock; keep left (west side) of the crest for easier going.

schedule.label: Scramble to the summit
schedule.detail: 3rd-4th class sections with exposure; most parties top out by late morning to early afternoon.

schedule.label: Begin descent
schedule.detail: Reverse the ridge and downclimb carefully - loose rock and exposure demand as much care going down as up.

schedule.label: Back at the car
schedule.detail: Coasting the logging road downhill on a bike (if brought up) saves significant time and effort on the way out.

days.objective: Summit Skookum Peak via the Twin Sisters logging-road approach and olivine (dunite) ridge

itinerary.totalNote: A long but standard single day: roughly 9-11 hours car-to-car, ~14 miles round trip and ~4,200 ft of gain, mixing a steep logging-road approach with 2nd-4th class ridge scrambling on grippy olivine rock.

fitnessSpec.hiking: strong all-day fitness - long approach/scramble day, and materially longer if the timberland gate is closed and the road must be walked or biked in
fitnessSpec.packWeight: light scramble day-pack, roughly 15-25 lbs (water, layers, light rack if linking with roped sections)

partner_requirements.approachTime: long - several hours to the ridge under normal conditions; add 2-4+ hours round trip if the timberland gate is locked and the road must be hiked or biked
requiredSkills: Class 3-4 scrambling movement on steep, exposed slab
route-finding on unmarked climbers' paths and old logging-road networks
navigation via map/GPS on gated, sometimes unsigned timberland roads
mountain-bike handling useful if the access gate is closed
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: solid, prior Class 3-4 scrambling experience with real exposure; partner should be comfortable moving unroped on steep slab and confident downclimbing the same terrain, since this is often linked with roped 5.4 pitches (Jaw's Tooth) on the same outing

before.permit: No climbing permit; the approach crosses private and DNR timberland - check current access, and carry a Discover Pass where parking on DNR land.
obj_haz: long approach on gated logging roads
before.bail: Descend the ridge to the approach roads and walk out.

access.fees: $5 daily or $30 annual Northwest Forest Pass.
access.rules: Standard Forest Service dispersed-use/Leave No Trace rules apply for day use and backcountry camping; respect gate closures on privately owned logging spurs off the main road.
access.permit: No day-use climbing permit required; standard Mount Baker Wilderness group-size/LNT rules apply.
access.closures: FSR 38, the primary access road, was significantly damaged in the December 2025 floods; as of mid-2026 the Forest Service (per District Ranger Louis Neff) has no published repair timeline for it. The unofficial log crossing with rope handrails over the Middle Fork Nooksack at the Elbow Lake trailhead was also destroyed in the same storms and has not been replaced. Even in a normal year, FSR 38 has a seasonal gate at Wallace Creek, about 1.3 miles before the trailhead, closed roughly December 1 through June 15.
access.landManager: U.S. Forest Service — Mount Baker Ranger District, Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Sedro-Woolley, WA). The logging-road approach network also crosses land held by private timber and olivine-mining interests (including Olivine Corporation holdings), and relations over road access have historically been contentious — some spurs are gated at the landowners' discretion.
access.land_manager: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Mount Baker Ranger District) — Mount Baker Wilderness
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at most trailheads — $30/year or $5/day.
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass (or an America the Beautiful / National Parks pass) displayed at the Elbow Lake Trail's north trailhead (FSR 38) — a separate trailhead from Pioneer Camp, which is on the trail's south end via Baker Lake Highway/FSR 12.

overnight_permit.where: Camping is on unregulated Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest and private timberland; no wilderness permit or registration is needed. The Dailey Prairie logging-road gate is separately locked to vehicles by the timber company, which is an access issue unrelated to camping.

weather.typical: Typical North Cascades summer alpine weather - generally mild and dry in the Jul-Sep window
weather.probability: Isolated afternoon thunderstorm buildups possible, especially August; wet weather in shoulder months makes the gated timberland approach roads slick and can worsen washouts, compounding gated and uncertain road access

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Significant fall exposure on the steep dunite/olivine slabs; grippy rock reduces slip risk but a fall from exposed sections would be consequential, and the long, remote day amplifies the cost of a mistake or injury
seasonal_hazards.crevasses: N/A - no glacier travel on this route (Twin Sisters' glaciers lie on other aspects of the range and are not crossed on this scramble)

before.approach: From the Mount Baker Ranger District office in Sedro-Woolley, drive north on WA-9 to Acme, turn right (east) on Mosquito Lake Road for about 9 miles, cross the Middle Fork Nooksack River, and continue onto Forest Road 38 for roughly 11 miles to the Elbow Lake Trail's north trailhead (a separate trailhead from 'Pioneer Camp,' which is actually on the trail's south end via Baker Lake Highway/FSR 12). From there, follow Elbow Lake Trail #697 (~8 miles, passing Lake Doreen) to Elbow Lake, then pick up the unmaintained Green Creek climbers' path into the Green Creek Cirque beneath Skookum's north/east flank before gaining the ridge. As of mid-2026 this whole approach is compromised: FSR 38 was damaged in the December 2025 floods with no published repair date, and the unofficial log crossing with rope handrails over the Middle Fork Nooksack near the trailhead was also washed out — confirm current conditions with the Mount Baker Ranger District before driving in.

approach_variants.name: Green Creek Cirque and the ridge from South Twin
approach_variants.notes: From the north trailhead of the Elbow Lake Trail, follow the maintained trail past Lake Doreen to Elbow Lake, then pick up the unmaintained, sparsely blue-blazed Green Creek climbers' path where it leaves at a switchback near Hildebrand Creek — it is easy to walk past. The path climbs into the Green Creek Cirque; treat the creek at the cirque mouth as the last reliable water. Loose third and fourth class scrambling out of the cirque gains the ridge crest just south of South Twin, and the route then follows the connecting ridge south. The road and the river crossing at the trailhead have both been damaged by flooding, so confirm access before driving in.
approach_variants.season: Midsummer to early autumn, once the cirque slabs are dry
hazards: Unbridged Middle Fork crossing at the trailhead, unfordable at high flow
Loose third and fourth class ground gaining the ridge out of the cirque
Immense exposure on the knife-edge sections of the ridge itself
approach_variants.baseFinding: Skookum sits on the ridge running SOUTH from South Twin, and the tower immediately north of it is Jaws' Tooth — a slender detached spire that reads as a tooth rather than a summit and is the single best identifier on this stretch of crest. The base of Skookum's north ridge is the notch on the far, southern side of that tooth, and it is normally reached by rappelling off the tooth rather than by walking to it; that rappel is the proof, because the crest between South Twin and Skookum does not simply go on foot. The rock is the second confirmation: the whole ridge here is reddish-orange olivine, coarse and startlingly grippy, and the ridge above the notch climbs on small positive edges with big air on both sides. If you are still down in the green, stream-fed Green Creek Cirque looking up at slabs, you have not gained the crest. If the summit in front of you is the high point of the whole range with everything else below it, that is South Twin, not Skookum.

waypoints.name: Elbow Lake Trail - North Trailhead (FR 38)
waypoints.note: Low-elevation trailhead off FR 38 via Mosquito Lake Rd; Northwest Forest Pass required, and FR 38 is gated Dec 1-Jun 15 at Wallace Creek. This is a separate trailhead from 'Pioneer Camp,' which sits at the trail's south end off Baker Lake Highway/FSR 12.
waypoints.directions: From the Mount Baker Ranger District office in Sedro-Woolley, drive north on WA-9 to Acme and turn right (east) onto Mosquito Lake Road for about 9 miles, crossing the Middle Fork Nooksack River, then continue onto Forest Road 38 for roughly 11 miles to the north trailhead for the Elbow Lake Trail at about 2,000 feet. A Northwest Forest Pass is required, and FR 38 is gated at Wallace Creek from December 1 through June 15. Do not confuse this with the Pioneer Camp trailhead, which sits at the trail's south end off the Baker Lake Highway (FSR 12). As of mid-2026 FR 38 was damaged in the December 2025 floods with no published repair date, so confirm current road conditions with the Mount Baker Ranger District before you drive in.

waypoints.name: Middle Fork Nooksack River crossing
waypoints.note: No bridge on this side — cross via an unofficial log/rope rig a few hundred yards up or downstream; can be unfordable at high flow, and the log has washed out in past seasons.

waypoints.name: Green Creek climbers' path junction (Hildebrand Creek switchback)
waypoints.note: Unmaintained, sparsely blue-blazed climbers' trail for Green Creek Cirque splits off the maintained Elbow Lake Trail #697 at a switchback near Hildebrand Creek — easy to walk past, watch for paint blazes and flagging.

waypoints.name: Green Creek at the cirque mouth
waypoints.note: Green Creek runs clear here at the entrance to the Green Creek Cirque — treat this as the last reliable water before the upper slabs and summit ridge.

waypoints.name: Connecting ridge gain point south of South Twin
waypoints.note: Loose, engaging 3rd/4th-class scrambling out of the cirque gains the ridge crest just south of South Twin; from here the route turns south along the connecting ridge to Skookum on grippy olivine.

waypoints.name: Skookum Peak summit
waypoints.note: True summit (also known as 'Kloke Peak'); descend by reversing the ridge and climbers' path back to the Green Creek Cirque.
